Core Error Callback Behavior

Core Error Callback Behaviors provide a controlled, observational mechanism for responding to finalized Vault error conditions. They execute after error normalization and state commitment, allowing legacy or convenience callbacks to observe error events without influencing pipeline execution or error authority.

Error Callback Contract Summary

  • Error callbacks are observational only and must not transform errors
  • Error callbacks must not throw or rethrow errors
  • Error callbacks receive the finalized VaultErrorShape
  • Error callbacks receive an immutable state snapshot
  • Callback execution does not affect error finalization or state commitment

The Core Error Callback contract guarantees that callback execution is isolated and non-authoritative. Callbacks are invoked only after the error state has been fully normalized, transformed, and committed. Any failures within callbacks are contained and do not alter the committed error state or pipeline outcome.

Core Error Callback Behaviors do not participate in error normalization, transformation, pipeline control, or scheduling. Their sole responsibility is to provide a compatibility and observation surface for already-finalized error conditions.

Add-on Error Callback Behaviors

In addition to core error normalization and transformation, FeatureCells may opt into add-on error callback behaviors. These behaviors observe the finalized VaultErrorShape after it has been committed to state and may perform supplemental, observational handling such as logging, diagnostics, or compatibility callbacks. Error callbacks do not replace, suppress, or alter error finalization.

Legacy error callbacks exist solely for convenience and backward compatibility. The primary mechanism for observing and responding to errors is the reactive vault.state().error. Callback-based handling should not be relied upon for core application logic.

Fluent Errors() API

A FeatureCell may declare multiple error callbacks using the fluent .errors() API. This API accepts an ordered array of error callbacks that are executed sequentially after the error state has been finalized. Callback registration occurs during FeatureCell initialization.

Error callbacks are strictly observational. They do not influence pipeline control flow, do not transform the error, and always return VAULT_NOOP.

An empty errors array is ignored and has no effect on pipeline execution.

Engineer-Supplied Error Callbacks

Error callbacks are supplied by engineers during FeatureCell initialization and execute exclusively after the authoritative error state has been committed. Each callback receives the normalized VaultErrorShape and an immutable state snapshot. Callbacks must not throw, must not mutate state, and must not attempt to resume pipeline execution.

Note

Although multiple error callbacks may be composed, callback logic should remain narrowly scoped and observational. Complex or interdependent callbacks can obscure intent and complicate failure analysis. Error callbacks are most effective when limited to logging, diagnostics, or transitional compatibility concerns.

Diagrams
Configuration

Error callbacks are configured separately from error normalization and transformation. When declared, the FeatureCell registers a core error callback behavior that executes after the error has been finalized and committed to state. Error callbacks are attached exclusively through the fluent .errors() API during FeatureCell initialization.

Error callbacks are optional and observational. They do not participate in error normalization, do not transform the VaultErrorShape, and do not influence pipeline control or state commitment. Their execution is isolated and failures within callbacks do not affect the authoritative error state.

Error Callback Patterns

Error callbacks permit side effects, but they execute after error finalization and must not influence pipeline control or state. Because of this, function structure, binding discipline, and isolation are especially important.

The following categories describe supported and discouraged error callback patterns, ordered from most to least preferred.

Category A: Pure / Context-Free Functions (Recommended)

Pure error callbacks depend only on their inputs and perform deterministic, observational side effects. They do not reference instance context and do not close over mutable external state.

This is the safest and most reusable callback form.

Example 1: Pure Error Callback

{{`employeeCell.errors(
  [
    (error: VaultErrorShape, state: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) => {
      console.info('Error occurred:', error.message);
      console.info('Current state value:', state.value);
    }
  ]
).initialize();`}}

Example 2: Factory-Generated Pure Error Callback

{{`export function createErrorLogger(label: string) {
  return (error: VaultErrorShape, state: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) => { => {
    console.info(label, error.message);
  };
}

employeeCell.errors(
  [
    createErrorLogger('EmployeeCell')
  ]
).initialize();`}}

Category B: Instance-Aware but Correctly Bound Callbacks (Acceptable)

Error callbacks may reference instance-owned configuration when properly bound. These callbacks remain deterministic per FeatureCell instance and must not be shared across cells.

Example 3: Arrow Function Using Instance State

{{`readonly prefix = '[Employee Error]';

readonly logError = (
  error: VaultErrorShape
) => {
  console.info(this.prefix, error.message);
};

employeeCell.errors(
  [this.logError]
).initialize();`}}

Example 4: Bound Instance Method

{{`public logError(
  error: VaultErrorShape,
  state: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>
) {
  console.info('Error:', error.message);
  console.info('Snapshot value:', state.value);
}

employeeCell.errors(
  [this.logError.bind(this)]
).initialize();`}}

Category C: Delegating Callbacks

Error callbacks may delegate work to helper functions as long as delegation remains observational and does not rely on external mutable state.

Example 5: Delegated Error Logging

{{`function logErrorMessage(error: VaultErrorShape) {
  console.info('Logged error:', error.message);
}

employeeCell.errors(
  [
    (error: VaultErrorShape) => logErrorMessage(error)
  ]
).initialize();`}}

Category D: Inline Lambda Callbacks (Allowed, Use Sparingly)

Inline callbacks are allowed but should remain trivial. Inline lambdas make it easy to accidentally introduce hidden coupling or complex logic.

Example 6: Inline Conditional Callback

{{`employeeCell.errors(
  [
    (error: VaultErrorShape) => {
      if (error.status === 404) {
        console.info('Resource not found');
      }
    }
  ]
).initialize();`}}
Error Callback Anti-Patterns

Error callbacks are observational hooks. They exist to react to finalized error state, not to influence pipeline execution or state. Misuse can introduce hidden coupling, degraded performance, or incorrect assumptions about error handling guarantees.

Common Anti-Patterns

  • Mutating the error or state snapshot
  • Performing long-running, blocking, or asynchronous work
  • Embedding business logic or decision-making
  • Depending on external mutable or shared state
  • Assuming callback execution affects pipeline flow or recovery

Violations in error callbacks are not always mechanically detectable. Issues typically surface as subtle bugs, degraded observability, or incorrect mental models of pipeline behavior.

Example: Discouraged Mutation Inside an Error Callback

{{`employeeCell.errors(
  [
    (error: VaultErrorShape, state: StateSnapshotShape<Employee[]>) => {
      // ❌ Mutating the finalized error
      error.message = 'Modified message';
      console.info('Error message:', error.message);
    }
  ]
).initialize();

// ❌ Violates the error callback contract: error and state are immutable snapshots`}}

Even if such mutation appears to have an effect, it violates pipeline guarantees. Error callbacks must treat both the error and state snapshot as immutable and authoritative.

Error Callback Summary

Error Callback Comparison

The following table summarizes the practical differences between the error callback styles demonstrated above. While all valid examples may execute correctly, they differ in reusability, testability, and long-term safety.

Error Callback Characteristics
Dimension Examples 1 / 2
Pure / Factory Callbacks 		Examples 3 / 4
Instance-Bound Callbacks 		Example 5
Delegating Callback 		Example 6
Inline Lambda
Purity ✅ ⚠️ Instance-scoped ⚠️ Depends on delegate ⚠️
Determinism ✅ ⚠️ Per instance ⚠️ Delegate-dependent ⚠️
Safety for Pipelines ✅ ✅ ⚠️ ⚠️
Reusability High Medium Medium Low
Testability High Medium Medium Lower
Risk of Accidental Closure Low Low Medium High
Intended Lifespan Long-lived Instance-limited Contextual Ephemeral
Recommended Usage Preferred Acceptable Use with care Use sparingly

Summary Rule

Any error callback must either be referentially transparent or explicitly instance-scoped and bound. Functions that depend on external mutable state or unbound instance context introduce hidden coupling and should be avoided.

Callback Examples
{{`// app.config.ts

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService
      {  
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: [],
      },
      [
        // **Important**
        // Error Callback behaviors are not registered as part of the 
        // FeatureCell’s declarative configuration.
      ],
      [
        // opt-in Controllers 
      ]
    )
  ]
};

// bank-employee.service.ts

import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { FeatureCell, injectVault } from '@sdux-vault/angular';
import { Employee } from './employee.shape';

@FeatureCell<Employee[]>('employees')
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class EmployeeService {
  readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    this.vault.errors(
      [
        (error, state) => {
          // Observational side effect only
          console.info('Employee FeatureCell error:', error.message);
          console.info('Last known state value:', state.value);
        }
      ]
    ).initialize();
  }
}`}}

Example 2: Async Error Callback (Remote Logging)

{{`// app.config.ts

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService
      {  
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: [],
      },
      [
        // **Important**
        // Error Callback behaviors are not registered as part of the 
        // FeatureCell’s declarative configuration.
      ],
      [
        // opt-in Controllers 
      ]
    )
  ]
};

// bank-employee.service.ts

import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { FeatureCell, injectVault } from '@sdux-vault/angular';
import { Employee } from './employee.shape';

@FeatureCell<Employee[]>('employees')
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class EmployeeService {
  readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    this.vault
      .errors(
        [
          async (error, state) => {
            await logErrorToApi({
              feature: 'employees',
              message: error.message,
              stateValue: state.value,
            });
          }
        ]
      )
      .initialize();
  }

  async logErrorToApi(payload: {
    message: string;
    feature: string;
    stateValue: unknown;
  }): Promise<void> {
    await fetch('/api/logs/errors', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });
  }
}`}}
